ABSTRACT
This research investigates the immobilization of enzymes within porous materials of varying geometries, such as spherical and
cylindrical pellet-shaped catalysts. The study focuses on modeling enzyme reactions using reaction–diffusion equations that cap-
ture the irreversible Michaelis–Menten kinetics, emphasizing the nonlinear nature of the process. A distinctive feature of this
work is the incorporation of fractional derivatives to enhance the understanding of enzymatic reaction kinetics. To achieve this,
a novel computational framework utilizing Laguerre wavelets is developed to compute substrate concentrations and effective-
ness factors over a broad range of parameter values. The proposed Laguerre wavelet method (LAWM) is rigorously compared
against established analytical and numerical approaches, including the Hermite wavelet method (HWM), Taylor series method
(TSM), Adomian decomposition method (ADM), and the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method (RKM). The findings reveal a high
degree of accuracy and consistency across all methods, underscoring the reliability and efficiency of the LAWM. This study offers
new insights into enzyme kinetics within porous catalysts and highlights the potential of fractional-order models for advancing
biocatalytic applications. The outcomes provide a robust theoretical foundation for optimizing the design and performance of
immobilized enzyme reactors in industrial and biotechnological settings.

Introduction
Understanding the behavior of immobilized enzymes is essen-
tial, particularly when their catalytic processes deviate from stan-
dard reaction pathways, as seen in nonlinear Michaelis–Menten
kinetics. This understanding is critical for optimizing their per-
formance in diverse applications such as biocatalysts, enzyme
reactors, and biosensors. Nonlinear Michaelis–Menten kinetics
manifest in unique ways, such as substrate inhibition, where
excessive substrate concentrations hinder enzymatic activity,
or substrate activation, where higher substrate levels enhance
enzyme functionality.

The study of immobilized enzymes becomes even more intrigu-
ing when these enzymes are confined within porous cata-
lysts. This immobilization provides a structured microenviron-
ment that significantly alters their behavior compared with free
enzymes in solution. The interactions within these confined
spaces are influenced by the immobilization techniques and the
specific physical and chemical characteristics of the porous cat-
alyst. This controlled environment can lead to unique reaction
dynamics that are absent in free enzyme systems.

Additionally, the interplay of substrate concentration, reaction

highlights the need for innovative approaches to study these

adopted to solve these reaction–diffusion equations. These meth-
ods offer precise and efficient ways to explore the behavior of
immobilized enzymes, paving the way for enhanced designs of
biocatalytic systems and more effective industrial applications.
Jeison et al. [1] utilized simulation techniques to study the impact
of immobilization on a range of reaction kinetic models, offering
valuable insights into how immobilization influences enzymatic
behavior. Similarly, Galaction et al. [2] examined the interplay
between internal and external mass transfer during glucose fer-
mentation for alcohol production. Their study highlighted the
inhibitory effects of glucose and employed a specialized biore-
actor with stationary basket beds containing immobilized Sac-
charomyces cerevisiae cells. Margret PonRani and Rajendran [3]
provided a theoretical analysis of steady-state glucose concentra-
tions within packed-bed reactors. Their work not only introduced
a robust theoretical model but also shed light on the complex pro-
cesses occurring in immobilized enzyme systems. Joy et al. [4]
developed a mathematical framework to predict the concentra-
tion profiles of immobilized enzyme systems in porous spherical
particles. This model incorporated a nonlinear parameter that
accounted for the reversible nature of Michaelis–Menten kinet-
ics, further advancing the understanding of enzyme dynamics in
constrained environments.
Immobilized enzymes have emerged as a game-changer in com-
mercial applications due to their remarkable efficiency. Unlike
enzymes dissolved in a reaction medium, immobilized enzymes
offer a host of benefits, including cost-effectiveness, enhanced
stability, and ease of separation from the reaction mixture.
These advantages streamline the production of high-purity prod-
ucts. Arroyo [5] provided an in-depth exploration of various
enzyme immobilization techniques, shedding light on their influ-
ence on catalytic activity and the long-term stability of biocat-
alysts. In another notable study, Rajab Khalilpour and Reza
Roostaazad [6] proposed a sophisticated mathematical model
to evaluate the functionality of immobilized glucose isomerase
enzymes in packed-bed reactors. Their model integrates a mod-
ified Michaelis–Menten kinetics framework to describe enzyme
behavior while thoroughly investigating mass transfer phenom-
ena within biocatalyst particles and across the reactor column.
Traditional approaches relying on soluble enzymes in industrial
processes face significant limitations, making immobilization an
attractive alternative [7]. Immobilized enzymes are enzymes that
have been attached to an inert support material, which can be
organic or inorganic, such as silica or calcium alginate. This
method of immobilization not only offers structural reinforce-
ment but also improves the enzyme’s durability under vary-
ing environmental factors like pH and temperature fluctuations.
Such enhanced stability yields significant economic benefits and
allows for the operation of reactors with higher enzyme con-
centrations, as demonstrated in prior studies [8, 9]. Adjusting
hydraulic conditions in the reactor, such as increasing agita-
tion, can effectively minimize external mass transfer limitations
[10]. Typically, immobilized enzymes help mitigate internal mass
transfer constraints [11, 12], although this benefit is dependent
on the reaction’s kinetic mechanism and may not be universally
applicable to all enzyme systems. Interestingly, in some cases,
effectiveness factors exceeding unity can be achieved [13, 14]. The
advantages of immobilized enzyme systems include the ability to
reuse the catalyst, flexibility in reactor design, simplified product
recovery, and easier reactor management. Nonetheless, these sys-
tems are not without challenges, such as potential loss of enzyme
activity, diffusional barriers, and higher costs associated with the
setup and maintenance.
The evaluation of internal diffusion effects in heterogeneous
enzymatic systems involves calculating the effectiveness factor,
symbolized as 𝜂. This factor represents the ratio of the average
reaction rate within the particle to the reaction rate in the absence
of diffusion constraints. Mathematical frameworks, based on spe-
cific assumptions [13–15], are utilized to predict the effectiveness
factor for these systems. These models offer a detailed approach
to analyzing and quantifying how internal diffusion influences
enzymatic activity. Recent investigations by Rajendran and col-
laborators [14–17] have derived analytical solutions for substrate
concentration that apply across the entire range of Thiele mod-
ulus values. This research integrates Michaelis–Menten kinetics
under both irreversible and reversible reaction scenarios.

The capacity of wavelets to represent a broad spectrum of opera-

Wavelets are increasingly being utilized to address complex
computational problems across various disciplines. Rajaraman
and Hariharan introduced efficient wavelet-based spectral meth-
ods for tackling nonlinear and fractional differential equations
characterized by high computational complexity [18–22]. The
behavior of immobilized enzymes within porous catalysts was
examined by Rajaraman [23] using Hermite wavelet techniques.
To address challenges in modeling anomalous diffusion and infil-
tration, particularly involving variable-order fractional nonlinear
differential equations, Devendra Chouhan et al. developed gen-
eralized fractional-order Bernoulli wavelets [24].
For singular boundary value problems (SBVPs), Mohammadi and
Hosseini [25] demonstrated the utility of Legendre wavelets by
constructing operational matrices for derivatives. Similarly, Doha
et al. [26] proposed a Chebyshev operational matrix algorithm of
the second kind to solve Lane-Emden-type differential equations.
SBVPs frequently appear in applied mathematics and chem-
ical sciences, where they demand robust and efficient solu-
tion strategies. The Hermite wavelet-based Galerkin method
(HWGM) was shown by Angadi [27] to outperform alternative
approaches. Faheem et al. [28] devised a high-resolution Hermite
wavelet-based method for solving space–time fractional partial
differential equations (STFPDE).
The Laguerre wavelet method (LAWM) and Hermite wavelet
method (HWM) [27–31] are built upon the construction of
operational matrices for integration and differentiation, which
transform complex differential equations into a system of alge-
braic equations that is significantly easier to solve. These meth-
ods have been pivotal in simplifying computational processes
for a wide variety of mathematical problems. A particularly
notable application of LAWM and HWM is their use in estimat-
ing substrate concentration and the effectiveness factor within
the framework of irreversible Michaelis–Menten kinetics. These
methods have proven highly effective in capturing the nonlin-
ear dynamics of enzymatic reactions, offering both accuracy and
computational efficiency.
The results obtained through these wavelet methods have been
meticulously validated by comparing them against outcomes
from other established techniques, demonstrating their reliabil-
ity and precision. Moreover, the adaptability of these approaches
extends to fractional-order systems, enabling their application in
modeling scenarios where anomalous kinetics and diffusion pro-
cesses are observed. Their inherent capability to address bound-
ary conditions seamlessly makes them an indispensable tool for
tackling a wide range of nonlinear and fractional-order differen-
tial equations in science and engineering. This innovative combi-
nation of analytical rigor and computational efficiency positions
LAWM and HWM as cutting-edge tools in advancing both theo-
retical research and practical applications.
The LAWM offers a compact representation of functions with
rapid convergence due to the orthogonal nature of Laguerre
polynomials, reducing computational complexity. It is highly
effective for solving nonlinear differential equations with initial
conditions because of its flexibility in handling boundary lay-
ers and singularities. The method uses operational matrices of
derivatives to simplify complex differential operators, transform-
ing the problem into a solvable system of algebraic equations.
Compared with conventional numerical methods like finite dif-
ference or finite element, the LAWM achieves higher accu-
racy with fewer computational points by minimizing truncation
errors. Unlike purely analytical methods, it can handle nonlinear-
ities and nonhomogeneous terms more efficiently, and it avoids
the iterative divergence issues often encountered in semiana-
lytical approaches like perturbation methods. LAWM provides
high accuracy in solving nonlinear fractional-order differential
equations, particularly when fractional derivatives are involved.
Unlike semianalytical methods such as ADM, VIM, HPM, and
HAM, which often require iterative processes or perturbation
expansions that may converge slowly or face challenges with
complex nonlinearities, LAWM offers an exact solution frame-
work based on wavelet functions. This reduces the potential for
approximation errors and ensures reliable results. Because of its
compact and orthogonal nature, LAWM significantly reduces the
number of required computational steps compared with tradi-
tional methods like FDM, which can become computationally
intensive for large-scale problems. Additionally, although ADM,
HPM, and HAM involve iterative expansions, LAWM directly
computes the solution through matrix operations, resulting in
faster convergence and shorter computational times.
Enzyme immobilization within porous materials is a cornerstone
of biocatalytic applications, yet understanding and optimizing
their performance require accurate mathematical modeling that
captures the complexities of nonlinear reaction–diffusion phe-
nomena. Conventional integer-order models often fail to ade-
quately describe the anomalous diffusion and memory effects
inherent in enzymatic reactions, motivating the integration of
fractional derivatives for a more precise depiction of these
processes. Existing analytical and numerical methods encounter
limitations in efficiency and accuracy when solving nonlinear
differential equations, driving the need for innovative compu-
tational frameworks like the LAWM. By addressing these chal-
lenges, this research aims to bridge the gap between theory
and application, providing reliable tools to optimize enzyme
reactors and improve their performance in industrial and
biotechnological processes. The motivation lies in advancing the
theoretical understanding of enzyme kinetics while delivering
practical solutions to enhance the design and scalability of immo-
bilized enzyme systems.

Fractional-order models have been successfully applied across
various domains to analyze dynamic processes. For instance,
fractional models have been used to study the impact of intra-
cellular calcium dynamics on fibroblast cells [32] and the
role of calcium oscillations in hepatocyte cells [33]. Similarly,
fractional-order frameworks have been instrumental in exploring
disease dynamics, such as brucellosis transmission [34], hepatitis
C treatment mechanisms [35], and the spread of polio under
vaccination [36]. In cancer research, fractional models have elu-
cidated glioblastoma growth dynamics and their implications for
patient survival [37]. Fractional approaches have also uncovered
chaotic behaviors in calcium diffusion, such as in Parkinson’s
disease models using Hilfer fractional derivatives [38].
These studies demonstrate the versatility and effectiveness of
fractional-order derivatives in modeling complex biological phe-
nomena, emphasizing the importance of such approaches in
understanding enzymatic processes within porous catalysts. By
leveraging fractional-order reaction–diffusion equations, this
study seeks to advance the modeling of Michaelis–Menten kinet-
ics for immobilized enzymes. Additionally, recent research on
plastic waste models [39] and their effects on air pollution has
underscored the broader implications of fractional models for
addressing global challenges.
The aforementioned research papers collectively highlight the
transformative potential of fractional-order models in under-
standing complex biological and chemical processes. Inspired by
these advancements, this study seeks to explore the applicability
of fractional derivatives in modeling enzymatic reaction kinet-
ics within porous catalysts, thereby extending their use to the
domain of biocatalysis. The success of these models in provid-
ing accurate and insightful results across diverse applications
motivates the development of a novel computational framework
based on Laguerre wavelets to analyze reaction–diffusion sys-
tems. This work aims to contribute to both the theoretical under-
standing and practical optimization of immobilized enzyme reac-
tors, bridging gaps in the literature with robust comparisons to
existing methods.

When a chemical reaction occurs simultaneously with mass
transfer, the substrate concentration experienced by enzyme
molecules within the particle differs from that at the surface. This
variation arises because the substrate must diffuse through the
particle to reach the enzyme molecules, leading to a gradient in
concentration. As a result, the overall reaction rate inside the par-
ticle is lower than the rate that would be observed if there were
no diffusional limitations.
To quantify these internal diffusional effects, the concept of the
“effectiveness factor” is employed. The effectiveness factor is
defined as the ratio of the actual reaction rate within the parti-
cle to the theoretical reaction rate that would occur if the entire
particle were exposed to the surface substrate concentration. This
dimensionless parameter provides a measure of the efficiency
with which the enzymes inside the particle contribute to the reac-
tion, accounting for diffusional restrictions.
The effectiveness factor is influenced by several factors, including
the particle size, the substrate Thiele modulus, the shape of the
particle (slab, spherical, or cylindrical), and the reaction kinet-
ics. For larger particles or higher Thiele modulus values, diffu-
sional resistance becomes more pronounced, leading to a lower
effectiveness factor. Understanding and optimizing the effective-
ness factor is critical in catalytic and biochemical processes, as
it directly impacts the design and performance of immobilized
enzyme systems and porous catalysts.

Phase 3 (Fractional-Order Enzyme
Kinetics: Cylindrical and Spherical

Fractional-order derivatives have become increasingly signifi-
cant across diverse domains, particularly for systems that exhibit
memory effects or long-term dependencies. In control systems,
signal processing, and biomedical engineering, fractional deriva-
tives enhance the precision of models by capturing the memory
and hereditary properties of processes. Similarly, in physical and
biological sciences, fractional calculus provides powerful tools for
understanding complex phenomena such as anomalous diffusion
and viscoelastic behavior, which cannot be adequately explained
using classical integer-order models.
Fractional derivatives (orders 1/2 and 3/2) provide a more accu-
rate representation of the anomalous diffusion and memory
effects observed in enzyme kinetics, which are not captured by
integer-order derivatives. This enhances the modeling of complex
transport and reaction processes within porous materials. Unlike
integer-order derivatives, fractional derivatives account for the
history-dependent behavior of the enzyme–substrate interac-
tions, reflecting more realistic kinetics. This leads to a better fit for
experimental data, particularly in cases where traditional mod-
els fail to capture long-term memory effects. When using the
LAWM, fractional derivatives allow for a higher degree of accu-
racy in approximating the enzyme concentration profiles within
various geometries (e.g., spherical and cylindrical catalysts). The
wavelet method efficiently handles these fractional derivatives
by converting the differential equations into algebraic systems,
ensuring precise solutions with fewer computational resources.
The LAWM offers an efficient way to solve these models by
transforming complex fractional-order differential equations into
simpler algebraic equations. Comparing fractional-order results
with integer-order results helps demonstrate the computational
advantages and the ability of the LAWM to handle complex kinet-
ics more effectively.
Moreover, the versatility of fractional calculus extends to math-
ematical modeling, where it offers deeper insights into nonlocal
and scale-invariant systems. Its application in solving real-world
problems often reveals behaviors and relationships that remain
hidden in traditional approaches, making it indispensable for
modern science and engineering.

faster particle dispersion than conventional diffusion, which may
result from long-range interactions, complex geometrical struc-
tures, external forces, or enhanced particle mobility. To model
anomalous diffusion, the dimensionless mass balance equation
for substrate concentration is extended by incorporating frac-
tional derivatives.

strate concentration as it evolves over time and space. However,

fractional derivatives are integrated into the equation, provid-

kinetics. This approach captures the intricate dynamics of
enzyme–substrate interactions, including transient behaviors
and anomalous diffusion patterns commonly observed in porous
materials. By accounting for these complexities, fractional deriva-
tives offer a powerful tool for modeling the nonstandard diffusion
and reaction mechanisms inherent to immobilized enzyme sys-
tems, thereby enhancing the accuracy and applicability of the
reaction–diffusion model.

Concluding Remarks
This study employs the LAWM to model the behavior of
immobilized enzymes under internal diffusional constraints in
steady-state conditions. The LAWM solutions demonstrate excel-
lent accuracy compared with methods such as the HWM, TSM,
ADM, and fourth-order RKM. Sensitivity analysis underscores
the influence of diffusional restrictions, substrate concentrations,
Thiele modulus values, and kinetic mechanisms on the predicted
concentration profiles and effectiveness factors. The findings
emphasize the critical role of selecting optimal parameter com-
binations (𝜓𝑏and 𝜙) to achieve accurate predictions for immo-
bilized enzyme systems. The LAWM not only provides a robust
framework for analyzing concentration profiles and effectiveness
factors but also facilitates the evaluation of conversion efficien-
cies within reactors. Its computational efficiency and precision
make it a practical tool for optimizing reactor performance and
addressing challenges in enzyme immobilization. This research
advances our understanding of enzyme-based reaction–diffusion
processes and highlights LWAM’s potential as a reliable method
for designing and optimizing immobilized enzyme reactors. It
offers a novel perspective on how mathematical modeling can
improve the efficiency and functionality of biocatalytic systems.

Abstract: This research investigates the immobilization of enzymes within porous materials of varying geometries, such as spherical and cylindrical pellet-shaped catalysts. The study focuses on modeling enzyme reactions using reaction–diffusion equations that cap- ture the irreversible Michaelis–Menten kinetics, emphasizing the nonlinear nature of the process. A distinctive feature of this work is the incorporation of fractional derivatives to enhance the understanding of enzymatic reaction kinetics. To achieve this, a novel computational framework utilizing Laguerre wavelets is developed to compute substrate concentrations and effective- ness factors over a broad range of parameter values. The proposed Laguerre wavelet method (LAWM) is rigorously compared against established analytical and numerical approaches, including the Hermite wavelet method (HWM), Taylor series method (TSM), Adomian decomposition method (ADM), and the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method (RKM). The findings reveal a high degree of accuracy and consistency across all methods, underscoring the reliability and efficiency of the LAWM. This study offers new insights into enzyme kinetics within porous catalysts and highlights the potential of fractional-order models for advancing biocatalytic applications. The outcomes provide a robust theoretical foundation for optimizing the design and performance of immobilized enzyme reactors in industrial and biotechnological settings.
